scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Irish set dancing traces its origins to the nineteenth century, when the French quadrille was introduced to Ireland by the British Army.
Rural Irish communities appropriated these court figures, marrying them to indigenous musical traditions and high-tempo stepping.

In 1897, the newly formed Gaelic League actively discouraged set dancing, viewing its quadrille lineage as foreign and antithetical to nationalist cultural revival, choosing instead to engineer and promote céilí dances.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally integrated into rural house dances, seasonal agricultural celebrations, and domestic gatherings, set dancing served as a core communal recreation separate from the codified solo step-dancing circuit.

Following its post-1980 revival, set dancing functions as a widespread international social pastime across Ireland, the Commonwealth, and continental Europe, uniting hobbyists at weekend workshops, festivals, and multi-day summer camps.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The standard social set dance is performed by eight dancers arranged as four couples facing inward on the four sides of a square, though two-couple variations called half sets also exist.

The couple with their backs to the band is designated 'First Tops', directly facing 'Second Tops'; 'First Sides' traditionally stands on the left of First Tops (or on the right in western regions like Connemara), facing 'Second Sides'.
Watch for Battering, Tops and Sides Rotation.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Social sets are danced to traditional Irish dance music, predominantly reels, jigs, polkas, and hornpipes, alongside less common mazurkas.

Historic solo set dances are linked to specific melodies featuring irregular phrase lengths or metrical peculiarities; nineteenth-century musical collections noted tunes like 'The Ace and Deuce of Pipering' and 'The Job of Journeywork' as benchmark pieces for solo dancers, played on bagpipes and fiddles.
Listen for the Fiddle, Uilleann pipes, Accordion, Tin whistle.
The pulse is 4/4, 2/4, 6/8, 9/8, or 3/4 depending on the figure.

A high-speed acoustic ensemble featuring driving fiddle, box, or pipes playing regular 8-bar dance strains, underscored by the heavy, rhythmic clatter of flat-soled shoes battering timber or stone floorboards.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historically danced in domestic rural kitchens and homesteads, the acoustic properties of the setting were deliberate: households sometimes positioned a cast-iron pot beneath the hearth flagstones to serve as a sound chamber for foot percussion.
Today, social sets take place primarily at community dance gatherings known as céilithe (or 'céilí and old time' events) and summer schools, such as the Willie Clancy Summer School in County Clare.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Connie Ryan was the central figure of the 1980s revival, responsible for researching, collecting, and reintroducing dozens of neglected regional sets across Ireland.

Historical collectors P.W. Joyce (1873) and J.G. O'Keeffe and Art O'Brien (1934) documented the solo and regional figure traditions, while modern practitioner Pat Murphy compiled core repertoires in landmark manuals.
Sets are strongly local and typically bear the names of parishes, towns, or counties.
Derived from the French court quadrille and adapted into nineteenth-century Irish rural folk culture, social set dancing evolved in parallel with Irish traditional step dance and solo sean-nós.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Set Dance is parent of Quadrille: Nineteenth-century French court quadrilles were adapted by Irish rural communities into set dances.
Set Dance is sibling of Irish stepdance: Shares footwork techniques and solo traditional set dance choreographies like 'The Blackbird'.
Set Dance is influence of Sean-nós dance: Influenced the percussive battering steps characteristic of County Clare set dancing.
Set Dance is variant of Ceili dance: Promoted by the Gaelic League as a nationalist replacement for quadrille-derived set dances.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright, grounded torso with arms held loosely or in couple ballroom hold; low center of gravity without stiff arching.
Partner holds during couple movement; loose natural carriage at sides or linked arms during figures.
Torso remains upright and relatively steady while the legs produce percussive foot rhythms.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
